cells.tense: You're the one choosing the line, and you already know what holding it has cost.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've carried well and call it finished today — to one person, plainly — and let that hand be free for what's next.
cells.core:
Choosing direction is what you do, and it doesn't come with wobble. You've usually counted the cost before you move, which is why endings don't scare you and picking up the next thing comes easy when it's easy. You finish what you start, and you can put a finished thing down.

What this is free to feed is smaller than it sounds. Pick the thing you've carried well, say it's over this week or set the date it's over, and tell one person the date. The held thing and the next thing can't both use the same hand. A good ending leaves more behind than people expect.
cells.sheetLine: You've carried it to the end and you know what it cost. Something's free now.
cells.verb: directing the fire with full knowledge of what it costs

cells.tense: You're standing at an ending that hasn't arrived, bracing for the cost of something you haven't begun.
cells.ask: Write one question about this you actually don't know the answer to, and leave the decision alone until you've answered it.
cells.core:
You decide something and you're already paying for it in your head. Maybe you've barely started and you can see the whole bill and you're holding your breath. Letting go is a skill you have; pointed forward it grips instead of releases, and the grip costs you the one step you could take today. Yet the same steadiness shows through whenever you start something and let it run a while before you judge it — a decision made, set down, lived with.

Wanting more information beats wanting the close. Write the question you can't answer and make answering it today's work. No deciding until it's answered.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that shut a while back, still facing it.
cells.ask: Do one piece of the thing at hand today — a plate in the sink, a line on the page — and stop the moment it's finished.
cells.core:
You know how to hold a line and right now you're not holding this one. Something behind you ended without a close, so the release didn't come, and waiting is what's sitting where a decision would be. Elsewhere the directing is still steady; you've just stepped out of this one.

The way back is small and physical, not a bigger decision. Do one piece of the thing in front of you, finish it, take one honest look at the finished shape. Do it again tomorrow. Pieces that end are how the ability to hold comes back without a hard push.

cells.tense: You keep saying it's all circumstance while your own hand is on the wheel and you're not claiming it.
cells.ask: Fix one thing that makes where you are easier to stay in — a chair, a meal, ten real minutes off a screen — and say out loud that you chose it.
cells.core:
You've been deciding things and telling yourself they just arrived — the job, the move, the no. The picking is still running; the saying-so isn't. You're directing more than you know, which is why the smallest repairs land harder than they should. Someone doing this with their eyes open would have a straight answer ready for where things are going, and would have said it out loud at least once.

Look at one thing you tend and say what you actually did to get where you are. Start with the smallest useful thing — a place that helps the real thing grow. Say the choice out loud to one person, or once privately to yourself. It gets easier once you stop pretending someone else is driving.

The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is the Too Much line about re-deciding what's already settled, which sounds clever and diagnoses; I'll keep it plain and at what a person does. The asks all stand as acts even if I'm wrong about which one fits, because each one is doable at a table today and teaches something either way.
